finding: The first scorecard's 'survey noise' bar had been estimated, not computed.
fix: Computed it from the survey data before publishing.

finding: Small-survey results averaged five samples before scoring and were scored against people included in the sample, so 300 people looked like 1,500 (claimed 1.3 points off).
fix: Re-scored against people not in the sample: 3.2 points off. Corrected docs 06 and 07, the results and the page.

finding: The track-record pooling experiment had the same scoring flaw.
fix: Fixed the scoring code and re-ran; small-group gains became clearer (Indian Singaporeans 8.2 to 2.9 points).

finding: US record citizens had never been compared with the chatbot on the same questions.
fix: Ran the test: record citizens 1.8 points off against the chatbot's 2.3.

finding: The page said the chatbot is good at drafting questions and finding past ones. Neither was tested; question-finding used a separate matching tool.
fix: Removed the claim.

finding: Terms (chatbot kind, record citizens) were used before they were defined, and 'closest question' was jargon.
fix: Re-ordered the page so every term is defined first; replaced the jargon with a plain rule.

finding: 'Worst cases' sounded negative.
fix: Replaced with 'standout groups' and 'most groups' everywhere.

finding: 'As people over 60 often do' was not supported: people over 60 were the most distinctive group on 0 of 20 Singapore questions.
fix: Replaced with Malay Singaporeans and young adults (6 and 5 of 20), and made the point general.

finding: The bullets describing the chatbot kind and record citizens said the same thing.
fix: Rewrote them to say how each works out group differences.

finding: Lower-case 'no AI' read as 'no AI at all' where it named the comparison column.
fix: Capitalised 'No AI' wherever it names the column.

finding: The pilot said to check against a larger survey, which is circular.
fix: Split-sample pilot: survey 600, let record citizens fill in groups from 300, compare with all 600.

finding: The job-worry figure had no source shown, and the Singapore survey overlapped COVID's arrival (November 2019 to March 2020).
fix: Traced to the World Values Survey file, added the fieldwork dates, and removed the example.

finding: Grey label text (section labels, table headings, notes, chart ticks) had 3.3:1 contrast in light mode; 4.5:1 is the minimum.
fix: Darkened the grey to 5.0:1. Dark mode already passed.

finding: Headings skipped levels (main title straight to third level), which confuses screen readers.
fix: Section labels became second-level headings; the chart title fourth level; the analysts' section a heading.

finding: Tables had no captions.
fix: Added captions: visible on the main tables, read-aloud only in the analysts' section.

finding: The chart told the chatbot kind and record citizens apart by colour only, apart from the legend.
fix: Labelled the first pair of bars directly.

finding: 'As accurately as a survey twice the size' overclaimed: 2.7 to 2.9 points against 2.6 to 2.7.
fix: 'About as accurately' in the short answer, the box, rule 1 and the README.

finding: The record-citizens box said the woman 'answered about 80 questions'. The survey has about 290; we used about 80.
fix: Now 'answered a long survey about her views and values'.

finding: Two tables headed the column of group names 'Points off'.
fix: Renamed to 'Group' and 'Country and groups'; the unit moved to the caption.

finding: The analysts' note dated the Singapore survey '2020'.
fix: Now gives the fieldwork window, November 2019 to March 2020.

finding: The page's language setting cannot be set from inside the page; the publishing wrapper adds the page frame.
fix: None possible here; screen readers default to the viewer's language.

finding: On this casebook page, the tag and link colours were below 4.5:1 as text.
fix: Added darker text versions of each colour for light mode and lighter ones for dark mode.

finding: Some 'less error' percentages were worked out from the rounded table figures. Singapore's most-groups figure for record citizens showed 27%; from the unrounded results it is 25%.
fix: Recomputed every percentage from the unrounded results and rebuilt the table, chart, chart labels and rules from them.

finding: The rows labelled 'standout groups' were not standout groups. They were the average over all groups, while 'most groups' was the middle result over all groups, so the same groups were shown twice, measured two ways.
fix: Defined standout groups as the quarter of group answers furthest from the national average on each question, and most groups as the rest, then recomputed. This changed the story: in Singapore the chatbot kind does not help most groups (4% more error) but helps standout groups about as much as record citizens (43% against 40%). The table, chart, so-what bullets and rules 2 and 3 were rewritten to match.

finding: '300 real people + AI = 600 real people' came from record citizens and the chatbot kind combined, but the page credited record citizens alone.
fix: The box caption and rule 1 now say record citizens do most of the work, with the chatbot kind weighted in by its track record.

finding: The example said record citizens use how often the woman prays. Prayer is not among the questions in the records we used.
fix: Changed to how often she goes to religious services, which is in the records, here and in the two-women example.

finding: The page implied a small survey needs only a few standard questions to link to the records. Our tests shared about 76; the minimum was never tested.
fix: Now says our tests shared about 76 questions and how few will do is not yet known.

finding: The survey-noise floor appeared as 1.4 in one place and 1.3 in another, and blind guessing as 14.7 against a rounded scale.
fix: Used the middle result everywhere: 1.3 for the floor and 15 for guessing blind, with the average shown beside it for analysts.

finding: 'Malay Singaporeans and young adults stood out most often' left out Indian Singaporeans, who stood out as often.
fix: Added Indian Singaporeans and named the United States' standout groups too: Republicans, Democrats and Black Americans.

finding: The page said as fact that the chatbot does well in the United States because American survey results are widely published.
fix: Now framed as the likely reason, with a second possibility added: the chatbot may already have seen these exact surveys.

finding: Rule 4 said online polls were far off. That rested on only 3 polls.
fix: Removed the claim.

finding: 'Even near-identical wording was 10 points off' rested on 2 of the 31 borrowed questions.
fix: Main text says 'about 10'; the analysts' table now notes that only 2 were near-identical.

finding: 'Records age, but group differences last longer than overall answers' was never tested.
fix: Removed. 'Records age' now says whether group differences hold up over time has not been tested.

finding: A simpler shortcut, filling in groups from age, sex, ethnicity and religion alone, came about as close as record citizens in Singapore on points off. The page did not say so.
fix: Added as a limit, with where record citizens still do better: the pattern of group differences, and the United States.

finding: Every small-survey test drew its people from the same survey as the records, so a survey run by a different firm in a different way was never tested.
fix: Added as a limit. The recommended pilot will show it.

finding: Several analysts' figures were off by rounding or mislabelled: the recipe range, the pooled results at 150 and 300, and column headings in statistics jargon.
fix: Corrected to 2.6 to 2.9, 2.9 and 2.6, and relabelled the columns 'Middle result' and 'Average'.

finding: The short answer said that outside the United States the chatbot helps only standout groups. Only Singapore was tested that way.
fix: Now says 'In Singapore'.

finding: A heading said the chatbot does not work in Singapore, but it cut the error for Singapore's standout groups by 43%. Rule 3 said it 'did nothing' for most groups; it made them 4% worse.
fix: Heading now reads 'works better in the United States than in Singapore'; rule 3 says 'did not help most groups'.

finding: The 1.3 tile said 'as close as a survey of this size can get', right after the 300-against-600 box, inviting the reading that 300 people could get that close.
fix: Now says even a full national survey is this far off from chance alone; the analysts' row says the same.

finding: '11 points off on average' and '8 points off' described middle results; the averages were 12.4 and 8.3.
fix: Now 'typically 11 points off' and 'typically 8 points off'.

finding: The analysts' note gave '3.2 and 2.9 points at 300' without saying what each number was.
fix: Now says 3.2 for a survey of 300 read straight off and 2.9 with record citizens alone.

finding: On phones the chart's labels were too small to read and crowded the bars.
fix: Moved labels above the bars, put the first row's names inside them and enlarged the phone font.

finding: On phones the small-groups table pushed its most important column, 'With AI filling in the group', off the right edge.
fix: Tightened table spacing on narrow screens. All four tables now fit a 375-pixel-wide phone without sideways scrolling.

finding: The contrast checker flagged the chart's in-bar labels as near-invisible in dark mode.
fix: Checked by hand: the labels sit on the coloured bars, not the background, at 5.1:1 or better. No change needed.

finding: The US most-groups No AI figure showed 3.2. The exact value is 3.146; it had been rounded twice (to 3.15, then to 3.2).
fix: Changed to 3.1. Saved the standout check as a script in the project (scripts/standout_split.py) so the figures come straight from unrounded results.

finding: Project document 07 rounded the pooled results up (3.0 and 2.7); the exact values are 2.946 and 2.647, as the scorecard shows.
fix: Corrected document 07 to 2.9 and 2.6.

finding: The page mixed three setups. The '300 + AI = 600' box and the small-groups table blended both kinds of AI with a small survey; the chatbot section started from the full survey's overall answer (the 'No AI' comparison); the short answer credited record citizens alone.
fix: Ran one test for every headline number (scripts/one_method_experiment.py: small surveys of 150, 300 and 600 drawn ten times, Singapore and the US, every method combined the same way, scored against the people not drawn) and rebuilt the page from it. Tables, chart and numbers in the text are now filled straight from its results.

finding: Under one method, 'the gain is biggest for standout groups' did not hold. Compared with the survey alone, standout groups gained no more than others (29% less error for both, Singapore, 300 people).
fix: Removed from the short answer and the rules. Kept as an analysts' note that explains why the earlier comparison showed it.

finding: The chatbot kind added nothing on top of record citizens in either country, so blending it into the headline was unnecessary.
fix: The headline now uses record citizens alone. Rule 3 says the chatbot adds nothing once record citizens are used. Revised by finding 58: for a brand-new question the chatbot does add.

finding: The limit 'a simpler shortcut came close' came from a different setup, and its model had no ethnicity in Singapore although the page said it did.
fix: Retested in the same run with ethnicity included: it did worse than record citizens at 150 and 300 people in both countries. Limit removed; result shown in the analysts' table.

finding: The page described record citizens learning from your own survey, for a brand-new question, but its result came from a different setup.
fix: Tested in the same run. A new section, 'A brand-new question', reports it: it helps, a little less than learning from past surveys.

finding: 'Our tests shared about 76 standard questions' was true for Singapore only; the US test used 83.
fix: Now 'about 80'.

finding: 'Typical group' was used without being explained.
fix: Defined in 'How we measure accuracy': half of all group answers land closer than this, half further off.

finding: The box read '2.7 points off against 2.7'.
fix: Now 'both are 2.7 points off'.

finding: In the new chart, end labels drifted away from their lines where values were close, and the chart's text was small on phones.
fix: Labels are centred on their points with a short coloured key; text enlarged on narrow screens.

finding: The chart's light-mode green has 2.8:1 contrast against the background, below 3:1 for chart marks.
fix: Kept: the palette checker passes it when every line is labelled directly and a table gives the same numbers, and both are on the page.

finding: The US 'record citizens from past surveys' learned from the same questions asked two years earlier. Reusing those answers directly did as well (2.4 points off) with no new survey, so the US '150 people beat 600' result showed reuse, not stretching a survey.
fix: Added last round's answers as its own route ('asked recently in the same survey: reuse those answers'). The US past-survey result no longer supports any headline claim.

finding: For a brand-new question the fair test is record citizens learned from your own survey, and the chatbot kind did about as well as them on their own. Combining the two had not been tested.
fix: Tested it in the same run: together they beat either alone with 150 people in both countries and with 300 in the US. The page is now organised around 'has your question been asked before?', and rules 2 and 3 were rewritten.

finding: Results were reported without uncertainty; some 'wins' were within chance (Singapore, 300 + AI against 600 alone: +0.02, range -0.36 to +0.25).
fix: 95% ranges from resampling questions and survey draws, a key-comparisons table on the page, 'about the same' for gaps within chance, and a new limit: gaps under about half a point are often chance.

finding: The questions are well known and their results published, so the chatbot may have read them.
fix: New limit: 'The chatbot may have had a head start'. The pilot tests its value on a truly new question.

finding: 'About as accurate for each group' held only for the typical group: 600 people alone did better for over-60s, 300 with AI better for Indian Singaporeans.
fix: Now 'for a typical group', with a sentence on how it varies group by group.

finding: '31% against 16%' for the chatbot in the US and Singapore was not a fair comparison: the US survey's weighting makes its survey-alone baseline weaker, and the difference crossed zero.
fix: Now argued from how much the chatbot counted (about 93 people per group in the US, 32 in Singapore) and its no-survey error (4.4 against 5.2), and softened to 'seems to'.

finding: The '1.3 best possible' figure came from a different setup. In this test the people checked against are a sample too, so even a perfect estimate scores about 1.5 points (Singapore) and 1.7 (US).
fix: Computed (scripts/yardstick_noise.py) and used 1.5 on the scale.

finding: Older figures (2 vs 61 countries, borrowed questions, published findings, 81/36/25%) sat beside the new test's numbers though they were measured differently.
fix: Labelled as earlier, separate tests in the text and in their own table, with a note not to compare them directly.

finding: 'The same budget buys twice the detail' ignored the standard questions each person must also answer.
fix: Now 'about half the people for the same detail, as long as the standard questions cost less than the people saved'.

finding: Analysts' tables: no-survey rows showed one size's value across all columns; differences shown to one decimal ('+0.0'); a label read 'Both of the above' with nothing above it.
fix: All three sizes shown, two decimals, and explicit labels. Added the comparisons that support each wording claim.

finding: When several sources were combined, capping each source's weight separately after fitting could distort the balance between them. It showed up as an odd result in a new combination (3.2 points off where each part alone did better).
fix: The cap now applies inside the fit. All runs were redone. Published figures were unchanged except two analysts' comparisons that moved by 0.01 to 0.02 points, now corrected on the page.

finding: Two figures in the write-up of the new tests were rounded from the wrong side of .x5 (3.75 shown as 3.7; 3.05 as 3.1).
fix: Checked the exact values: 3.8 and 3.0.

finding: Claude told King that "most people give the same answer only about 70-80% of the time". That is an average across people and questions, not most people, and the 81% figure in the methods notes had no source.
fix: Checked against the Stanford paper (81.25%, 1,052 US adults, two weeks apart) and our own Twin-2K-500 calculation (69%); corrected the wording and added both sources.

finding: The casebook gave the floor as about 1.3 points, a figure from an earlier test; the one-method scorecard uses 1.5 in Singapore and 1.7 in the United States.
fix: Casebook now matches the scorecard.

finding: The Twin-2K-500 loader labelled its groups from the wrong questions, shifted by one (region was read as age, sex as education, and so on). Only an old baseline used them.
fix: Labels corrected, a test added, and the baseline rerun: its average moved from 52.79% to 52.80%, and no published figure changed.

finding: The casebook still said about 4,100 lines of Python and 31 passing tests; the code has grown since.
fix: Recounted: about 4,800 lines in the code and scripts folders, 32 passing tests.

finding: The short answer said record citizens stretch a small survey best. For a brand-new question the two kinds of AI were within chance of each other at every survey size; record citizens clearly beat the chatbot only when the question had been asked before.
fix: Short answer and README rewritten to say exactly that; a build check now stops the page if the data stop supporting it.

finding: "300 with AI did better for the smallest groups ... and somewhat worse for people over 60": every group-by-group difference was within chance, and Malay Singaporeans came out the same.
fix: Reworded as varying within chance, with the Indian and over-60 figures read from the data (3.5 against 4.4; 2.8 against 2.3).

finding: The chatbot card described role-play ("You are a 62-year-old Singaporean woman"), but in the tests the chatbot was asked directly for each group's answers.
fix: Added: "In our tests, it was asked directly for each group's answers."

finding: The chatbot's worth (93 real people per group in the United States against 32 in Singapore) was explained by accuracy alone; part of the gap comes from US weighting, which makes each real answer count for less.
fix: Both reasons now given.

finding: Smaller points: a simple average of five chatbots was clearly worse only in the United States; near-identical borrowed questions were about 9 points off, not 10; Singapore's full set was 76 standard questions, not 80; the best possible was shown only for Singapore; the borrowed-question test had 20 groups plus everyone; the demographics note was wrong for the US; published findings were added to record citizens and the chatbot; a rerun needs a pilot.
fix: All corrected on the page and in the analysts' notes.

finding: "We call this the chatbot kind" could be read as naming the combination; "survey alone" and "filling in" were used before being defined; one paragraph used 81% for two different things; the combination of both kinds had six names; several sentences ran over 40 words.
fix: Short answer reordered; both terms defined in "How we measure accuracy"; one name, "both kinds of AI"; second 81% moved to the analysts' note; long sentences split.

finding: Results came before the explanation of how accuracy is measured; the three cases for choosing an AI were explained three times; the rules repeated the evidence; three limits all said "the pilot will show it"; a changelog note had been left in the analysts' section.
fix: Page reordered (measurement first), each finding said once, rules shortened to point back, pilot limits merged into one, note removed.

finding: No language set on the page; chart values reachable only by hovering or tabbing, on 8px targets; table headers at 11px on phones and some key text at 12px; row labels were not marked as headers.
fix: Language set; values printed beside every chart point; sizes raised to 12-13px; row labels marked as row headers. axe-core: no violations.

finding: The Singapore chart's two end labels overlapped; table text wrapped raggedly on phones; green marked both record citizens and the "good enough" card; the footer rule was shorter than the others; the "=" sat alone on phones; the comparisons table mixed both countries.
fix: Labels spaced, wrapping fixed, "good enough" card made neutral, footer full width, "is about as accurate as" on phones, one comparisons table per country with true minus signs.

finding: The casebook's downloadable interaction log had not been refreshed at the last publish, and the playbook and explainer skill still gave 1.3 points as the best possible.
fix: Package rebuilt with the page; notes corrected to about 1.5 to 1.7.

finding: The casebook had no page language set, tables that scroll sideways could not be reached by keyboard, the interaction timeline's labels were 8px, and a labelled group had no role.
fix: Language set, scrolling tables made focusable regions, labels raised to 11px, role added. axe-core: no violations on either page.

when: Making the scorecard easy to follow
finding: Version 47 showed about 3,600 words and 21 headings before the analysts' section; method and evidence came before what to do, and the same points appeared in several places.
fix: Rebuilt in layers: the answer, the caveats, what to do, how we know and limits on the main path, with detail in six folded sections one click away. About 2,000 words and 12 headings on the main path.

when: Making the scorecard easy to follow
finding: Five fresh readers playing a non-technical executive tripped on: what AI "fills in" when 300 people already answered; "both" in the headline; how a perfect estimate can be off; "standard questions", "records" and "scorecard" used before being explained; "similar people from where?"
fix: Each phrase rewritten in plain words at first use; record citizens' source named (World Values Survey, 2,012 people) and the model described as a statistical model, not a chatbot.

when: Making the scorecard easy to follow
finding: Readers found statements that seemed to contradict each other: "reuse last round's answers" against "don't borrow numbers"; "ask extra people from small groups" against "helps little with AI"; a brand-new product question quoted at 2.7 although products were not tested; "can't survey? run a survey".
fix: Each resolved: the exception is the same question in the latest round of the same survey; extra people help mainly without AI; numbers labelled as attitude questions; the no-survey case moved to step 3.

when: Making the scorecard easy to follow
finding: Readers could not act on the page: no worked example, the steps tangled (the same 2.4 appeared with and without a survey), the pilot had no pass test and no answer for a one-off 300-person budget, and the biggest caveats sat at the bottom.
fix: Added a worked Singapore example; reordered the steps; the pilot now has a pass test and applies to repeated topics only; caveats moved under the short answer and stated bluntly.

when: Making the scorecard easy to follow
finding: Readers still rated completeness low because the page cannot say what set-up costs, or how results change with a separately run survey or on products and prices: none of these has been tested.
fix: Stated plainly on the page as not yet known; needs a real pilot to answer.
